item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The idea started out with the fungus, which was ages ago posted as a failed article by someone back in 2012-13-ish. I came up with a plausible "scientific" mechanism for it back then, but I doubt anyone but me (maybe Michael Atreus, in the best sense possible) gets excited about equations enough to upvote on basis of that, which made it go on the backburner as a potential rewrite to be. Weaponization came to mind, but again, not something Foundation would do, and still kinda light. Then, I thought I'd use the innocuous little thing to showcase the intended GRU-P format during talks with Crayne.

And finally, one of those days, going home from work and thinking, I had the idea this could explain certain sorts of monster - I must say this "mythology put right" thing is kinda inspired by Charlie Stross ,especially the short story Concrete Jungle where he ends up 'explaining' gorgonism (yes, those gorgons from greek mythology).

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Reading density notwithstanding, this is a delightful example of extrapolation of a relatively simple starting idea to ingenious effect. Definitely something worth pointing to when people ask about what is meant by fleshing out basic concepts (and which I'll refer to myself when I'm having the same thoughts).

Out of interest in terms of writing mechanics, did the idea start with the fungus and work from there, or was the fungus added as the starting point in order to lead to the "real" idea?

Ah well.
I thought that the specific concepts included (GRU-P way of working; finding military and civillian use for a rather innocuous anomaly; a 'scientific' explanation for mythical hydras/dragons/multiheaded whatnot) would work well enough to pull the article. I guess they didn't.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Always nice to see more GRU-P stuff on the wiki, especially when it incorporates the feeling of Soviet executive reports.

Which I guess is the problem, in a way. This reads, both in format and content, like a scientific report. It's just that scientific reports, combined with the wall of text that Deci mentioned, don't make for compelling reading.

There's plenty of stuff I like in this (GRU-P in general, the attempts to create to find uses for it on a massive scale, the interview), but reading the article proper is a slog. No vote.

EDIT: fixed the wall-of-textness. To an extent, this was partly my fault for not having leading spaces on paragraph break liens after >

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This suffers from wall-of-text syndrome, and while I do want to upvote, I can't upvote wall text monsters due to how hard they are to read. I didn't edit them in cause I don't know what's not supposed to have line breaks and what isn't, so I figured I'd let you know.

Otherwise, this is good. Anything that makes GRU-Division-P more interesting is a bonus in my book, and I hope we get more content like this in the future.

EDIT: Also, is this supposed to be a tale or a new GoI Format kind of style?

item.content:encoded:
Something that's been lingering in my sandbox for about a year - a part of a dead in the water project with Crayne to make a working GRU-P hub and format after the one someone did for the contest ended up a failure. I wrote this while he was making a nice typewriter-on-yellow-paper CSS for it.

Well, I suppose I want to get a bit of closure in terms of seeing whether, as I said, this rock will fly.

Obviously thanks to Crayne for many plottings over IRC, and Kalinin and thedeadlymoose for proofreading this a year ago.
